items.title: [ScienceDaily] Keto diet slashes liver fat by 67% in just 4 months
items.content_html: A new clinical trial found that the ketogenic diet dramatically outperformed Mediterranean and low-fat diets in reducing liver fat and improving metabolic health, even when participants lost similar amounts of weight. After just four to five months, about half of those following keto no longer met the criteria for prediabetes, while their liver fat dropped by an average of 67%.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] For better mental health, how often you exercise may matter more than how hard
items.content_html: A study of more than 10,000 college students found that exercising regularly may be more important for mental health than pushing yourself through intense or lengthy workouts. Students who exercised less frequently were more likely to experience depression and anxiety a year later, suggesting that consistency could be a key ingredient in protecting mental well-being.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] A study of 30,000 people reveals which antidepressants may work best
items.content_html: A major review involving more than 30,000 people found that three antidepressants, including Lexapro and Cymbalta, may be more effective than Prozac at maintaining improvements in depression symptoms. However, limitations in the research and a lack of truly long-term data mean scientists still cannot say which antidepressant is best.

items.title: [medicalxpress.com] Michigan State studies link pregnancy stress patterns to maternal and infant outcomes
items.content_html: Researchers at Michigan State University found that stress during pregnancy was associated with higher levels of maternal depression six months after birth, while the timing of stress was linked to infants’ stress responses and temperament at six months. The studies tracked stress weekly beginning at 15 weeks of pregnancy to examine how exposure at different stages related to outcomes. The associations varied with the timing and consistency of stress and the child’s sex. The studies do not establish that stress caused the outcomes. The researchers are following the mothers and children into middle childhood to examine how early stress and supportive environments relate to development.

items.title: [bmj.com] Study finds limited code sharing as medical AI oversight faces scrutiny
items.content_html: Researchers from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Dana-Farber Cancer Institute reviewed nearly 4,000 clinical prediction studies and found that only about one in eight reported sharing code. Many public repositories also lacked documentation or files needed to run and check the analyses. The findings are intended to inform a guideline on reusable research code. A physician writing in The BMJ urged Utah to publish independently assessed counts of missed escalation cases before allowing AI-generated acne prescriptions to be reviewed after issuance rather than before. In South Korea, Doctors for a Fair Society called for scrutiny of possible AI-assisted cheating in a medical-school entrance exam, while the group’s leader cautioned against treating an individual’s high score or educational background as proof of wrongdoing.

items.title: [nacional.hr] ECDC urges hospital infection controls as resistant infections spread in Europe
items.content_html: The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) said on Nov. 18 that antibiotic-resistant infections continue to spread in Europe, leaving doctors with fewer effective treatment options. More than 70% of the health burden caused by antimicrobial resistance in Europe is linked to healthcare-associated infections, and stronger infection prevention could avert half of that burden, the ECDC said. The agency called for hand hygiene, protective equipment, prompt detection, isolation of infected patients and effective cleaning in healthcare facilities. It also urged better access to laboratories and adequate infection-control staffing. The ECDC highlighted avoidable antibiotic use for viral illnesses, particularly in children, while Germany’s Robert Koch Institute listed its new ARS-ResistenzCheck data tool among resources for clinical practice.

items.title: [gacetamedica.com] Neurologists urge Mediterranean diet as trial links ultraprocessed foods to brain changes
items.content_html: The Spanish Society of Neurology presented guidance on diet and brain health at its annual meeting in Seville, citing evidence for a Mediterranean-style diet and concerns about ultraprocessed foods. The society cited research linking adherence to a Mediterranean diet with at least 12% lower stroke risk and up to 30% lower Alzheimer’s disease risk. It also recommended regular mealtimes, cooking at home and limiting screen use during meals. Separately, a small Virginia Tech feeding trial found that participants aged 18 to 21 had a reduced response to a milkshake in the brain’s orbitofrontal cortex after two weeks on a diet dominated by ultraprocessed foods. Participants aged 22 to 25 showed no significant change. The study involved 22 people, and researchers said the age-related finding was exploratory. They plan to investigate whether the changes persist and examine effects in younger groups.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] A little-known protein could be a powerful weapon against Alzheimer’s
items.content_html: Scientists have uncovered a powerful natural defense against Alzheimer’s disease that could open the door to new treatments. By boosting a protein called SORLA, researchers significantly reduced toxic tau tangles, protected connections between brain cells, and prevented some of the brain shrinkage associated with neurodegeneration in mice. Removing the protein made the damage worse, highlighting its critical protective role.

items.title: [Reason] Age-Related Synaptic Dysfunction and Possible Approaches to Treatment
items.content_html: Dysfunction of the synaptic connections between neurons in the brain is characteristic of aging and exaggerated in neurodegenerative conditions, particularly Alzheimer's disease. The brain is a collection of neural networks: a neuron extends branching axons that connect to other neurons via synapse structures. When synapses lose function, the network loses function, and cognitive decline is the result. Here, researchers discuss the biochemistry of synapses and a variety of approaches to therapy that might improve matters. They conclude that the most promising approaches at the present time are those focused on reducing the impact of aging on the function of glial cells. items.title: [ecdc.europa.eu] European disease agency warns resistant bacteria threaten hospital treatment
items.content_html: The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) warned on Nov. 18 that antibiotic-resistant bacteria continue to spread across Europe, leaving doctors with fewer effective treatments. Its European Antibiotic Awareness Day alert called for urgent, sustained action. More than 35,000 people die each year from antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in the European Union and European Economic Area. More than 70% of Europe’s AMR health burden is linked to multidrug-resistant infections acquired in healthcare settings. The ECDC said resistant infections could make it harder or impossible to safely carry out organ transplants, cancer chemotherapy and intensive care. It called for coordinated infection prevention, careful antibiotic prescribing, stronger laboratory capacity and surveillance. Faster genomic monitoring can help track the spread of resistant strains and guide treatment decisions, it said.

items.title: [news-medical.net] Small study links appetite-suppressing drugs to low nutrient intake
items.content_html: A small exploratory study found that some people taking appetite-suppressing medicines such as Wegovy and Mounjaro consumed too little energy and key nutrients and had limited awareness of the potential shortfalls. Researchers asked 14 patients at one English general practice—10 treated privately and four through the National Health Service—to recall what they ate over two days. Average intake was 1,231 calories a day, or 58.5% of estimated energy needs; three participants reported less than 800 calories daily. Participants linked their reduced intake to appetite suppression and described a lack of structured follow-up and dietary advice. Researchers cautioned that the observational study, based on a small group from one relatively affluent practice, cannot establish cause and effect and may not apply widely.

items.title: [frontiersin.org] Kidney studies test earlier detection beyond routine clinical measures
items.content_html: A single-center study of 542 adults with type 2 diabetes found that a model combining routine clinical variables with the TyHGB metabolic index had moderate accuracy in identifying early diabetic kidney disease. The logistic regression model had an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.709 in a later patient cohort; adding TyHGB did not show a confirmed improvement in that cohort. The researchers said independent, multicenter testing is needed to establish the model’s calibration and clinical usefulness. Two other recent reports examine limits in kidney monitoring. A study of 1,200 cancer patients found that routine estimates of filtration rates could overstate kidney function around critical thresholds, potentially increasing chemotherapy toxicity. A postoperative case series proposes that urine-based biochemical measures may signal recovery from acute kidney injury (AKI) before serum creatinine falls, but calls for larger prospective studies.

items.title: [zdnet.com] AI agents expand cyber risks as companies struggle to enforce controls
items.content_html: Security experts warn that increasingly autonomous AI agents can move across company systems at machine speed, complicating conventional identity and access controls. Agents may query databases, call application programming interfaces, use tools or act through an employee’s account. Experts say a login record alone may not show who initiated an action or what the agent did. European Central Bank Vice-President Boris Vujčić said AI is increasing the scale and speed of cyberattacks, while banks face delays in adapting their defenses. Weill Cornell Medicine said an employee entered patient information into AI tools during a research study without authorization. A DNSFilter survey found that half of healthcare security leaders confirmed or suspected that employees had connected unapproved AI tools to critical systems. A Linux Foundation survey of 308 cybersecurity practitioners found that 58% said development teams release code faster than security staff can review it. Security specialists recommend giving each agent a distinct identity, limiting its permissions to a specific task, setting credentials to expire and recording actions for review. The Electronic Frontier Foundation, a digital-rights group, says established security practices could have prevented the OpenAI–Hugging Face incident and similar incidents. It calls for enforceable standards, independent investigations and notice to affected parties after incidents.

items.title: [gwec.net] Ember analysis says adding wind cuts reliable power costs 18%
items.content_html:
Adding wind to solar and batteries cuts the modeled median cost of meeting 90% of electricity demand from $105 to $86 per megawatt-hour, according to an analysis by energy think tank Ember published with the Global Wind Energy Council (GWEC). The combination reduces storage needs because wind and solar output vary at different times and across seasons. Ember estimated that three-quarters of global electricity demand could be met at the 90% threshold for under $100/MWh with wind, compared with half using solar and batteries alone.

The analysis also examines the economics of planned fossil-fuel capacity: of 845 gigawatts of coal and gas plants in planning, 706 GW are in regions where firm renewable electricity with backup could cost less than $100/MWh. Ember said it modeled hourly weather from 2015 through 2024 against constant demand and described the results as a stress test, not a forecast.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] A 19-year study reveals a troubling link between napping and death
items.content_html: A surprising new study suggests that when and how often older adults nap could reveal hidden warning signs about their health. Researchers followed 1,338 people for up to 19 years and discovered that longer, more frequent naps were linked to higher mortality, while morning nappers faced a 30% greater risk of death than afternoon nappers. Each additional hour of daytime sleep was associated with a 13% increase in mortality risk.

items.title: [The Guardian Global Development] ‘Crocodiles are possible, but hunger is certain’: Malawi’s foragers forced into infested waters
items.content_html:
Once ‘famine food’, empty granaries have forced people along the Shire River to harvest water-lily roots in waters full of the reptiles

The mid-morning heat in Malawi’s lower Shire River basin is already suffocating, but Beatrice Maseko cannot afford to look away from the water’s edge. Coated in grey, foul-smelling mud up to her thighs, the 34-year-old mother of four plunges both arms deep into the heavy sediment of a sprawling marsh. Her fingers feel blindly through the silt for the rough, bulbous roots of wild water lilies, known as nyika.

Around her, a dozen other women move with deliberate, hushed slowness. No one splashes; no one speaks above a tense whisper. Just 50 yards away, where the marsh opens into the main artery of the Shire River, the silhouette of a Nile crocodile glides silently beneath the surface.

items.title: [gacetamedica.com] Virus treatment improves survival in pancreatic cancer trial; experimental WRN drug shows activity
items.content_html: An international phase 2b trial found that adding the oncolytic virus VCN-01 to chemotherapy increased median overall survival to 10.8 months for patients with previously untreated metastatic pancreatic cancer, compared with 8.6 months for those receiving chemotherapy alone. Madrid’s Hospital 12 de Octubre led the 112-patient trial, and Nature Medicine published the results. A separate phase 1 study tested an experimental WRN inhibitor in advanced solid tumors with microsatellite instability or DNA repair deficiency. Among 66 evaluable patients, 74.2% had disease control and 10.6% had a confirmed partial response. Researchers said the early findings require confirmation in later trials.

items.title: [dailyausaf.com] Studies find Alzheimer’s warning signals years before symptoms emerge
items.content_html: Separate studies report changes in the brain, sleep, navigation and nerve-muscle communication that may appear before Alzheimer’s symptoms, but none establishes a routine early-detection test. A Johns Hopkins team found that the entorhinal cortex and amygdala shrank earlier and faster than the hippocampus, with tissue loss in those regions associated with local tau changes. A Stanford-led team used resting-state brain scans to develop an experimental score linked to faster cognitive decline, amyloid buildup and later diagnoses among more than 1,300 initially healthy adults followed for up to 12 years. Other research examined spatial navigation in 100 middle-aged adults at elevated dementia risk. A separate laboratory study found that familial Alzheimer’s mutations disrupted nerve-muscle communication in a model without a brain or spinal cord. A sleep study of 116 adults linked features of deep-sleep waves with cognitive changes over time. The findings come from distinct studies and require further validation; the Stanford score is not available for clinical use, and the nerve-muscle experiment used laboratory models.
